description:
Start with a real project

Record the intended final URL for each key page and the status you expect to see.

Review broken links and crawl findings

Group broken links by the pages that contain them. Fix links in shared templates first if the same error appears across many pages.

Check the final result

Recheck affected URLs after edits and confirm indexing separately where needed. A crawler finding and Google's index status describe different things.

Frequently asked questions

Which errors should I check first?

Start with issues that prevent customers or crawlers from reaching important pages.

Browse related tools on SEOGBTools.

Triage a crawl before assigning fixes

Start with the pages that bring readers to a product, answer a support question, or lead to checkout. Open a few examples from each crawl warning. A broken link in a shared footer can appear on hundreds of pages. Fixing that one footer link may solve more than editing dozens of descriptions. A broken link in a single popular guide may also deserve quick attention if readers use it to reach a product.

Record the source URL, the link destination, and what you see when opening it. If the destination was moved, update the source to the correct live page where possible. If there is no relevant replacement, remove the link or revise the sentence so it gives a useful next step. Run a focused crawl afterward and check the same examples in a browser.

Does a clean crawl mean every page is indexed?

Use the crawl to check what the crawler can reach and what it finds. Use Search Console to check the Google indexing status of specific URLs where needed.

What a Seobility website audit can tell you

A technical SEO audit starts with a practical question. Can someone open the page they came for and follow the links they need? A website crawler checks many URLs in a consistent way. It can surface broken links, redirects, and pages that need a closer look. Seobility gives you a place to review those findings and decide which ones to investigate.

Think of the first crawl as a record of what the crawler found at a particular time. Your store may be changing while it runs. A link might have failed while a product was being updated, or a new category may have gone live after the crawler passed it. Record the date, the starting URL, and any limits you used. These details make the next crawl easier to compare.

Before comparing Seobility group buy access with an official plan, list the tasks your team needs. A small store may want to check broken internal links after changing a menu. An agency may need separate projects and regular reports for several clients. Ask SEOGBTools which tools and limits apply to the current offer, especially if you rely on project history, exports, or a certain number of crawled pages.

Start with pages customers use

Make a short list of pages that matter to the business. Include the homepage, main categories, top products, and common help pages. Add pages that appear in campaigns or receive links from other sites. Give each URL a note describing what people come there to do. A reader who reaches a shipping guide should be able to find delivery estimates and return to the store.

Open a few of those pages by following links from the homepage. This shows you what a visitor sees and may reveal a problem before you open a crawl report. For example, a button could lead to a page that loads but describes a product that is no longer sold. A crawler may see a successful response. The person reviewing the page can see why the destination is a poor match.

Keep the list small enough to check manually. It can grow after the first review. A list of ten useful pages with clear next actions gives a team more direction than a long list of issues with no owners. If a customer journey has several steps, note where the next link appears and who can change it.

Check how the crawler reached each URL

Look at the pages where the crawler found a problem. The location can tell you how many people may run into it and how much work a fix will take. A broken link in a product description may need a single edit. A broken link in the main menu can appear on every page that uses the menu.

Record the source page, the destination, and the link text. If a page has several links to the same destination, note which one is broken or misleading. The same words can point to different URLs in different parts of the page. A screenshot or a short note about the section can help another person find the link quickly.

Check whether the source page is still intended for visitors. An old campaign can be publicly reachable even after it disappears from the navigation. If it continues to send readers to a current service, fix the link. If its role has changed, ask the page owner what readers should find there today.

Fix broken internal links where they start

Open the destination URL and check what happens. If the product moved to a new address, find the current listing and open it before changing the link. If the product is gone, decide whether a category or another guide helps the reader. Link to the replacement only if it answers the need described in the original sentence.

For a shared footer or menu, make the correction in the place that controls the shared link. Open several pages that use the template after you save it. Confirm the link text still fits the destination and the link works on a phone. If the same link appears in a separate article, check that copy independently.

A redirect can help people who already have the old address. An internal link can still point directly to the current address so visitors take fewer steps. If a link crosses more than one redirect before reaching the final page, record the chain in the audit notes. That can make it easier to find the source of a recurring issue after a migration.

Investigate indexability one page at a time

A crawl can help you notice pages that send signals about how they should be handled. Google Search Console can show the reported indexing status of an individual URL. When the two tools give different information, read the date and the exact URL in each report. The current page and the last version Google fetched may differ.

Check the address you meant to inspect. A product URL can look similar to a tag page or a variation URL. Open the version you want visitors to find and see whether it has the expected content. Review the canonical address and whether it points to the page your team treats as the main version. Where several URLs serve the same purpose, document which one should be used in menus and internal links.

Keep crawl access and indexing status separate in your notes. A crawler reaching a page shows that it could fetch the page under the settings used. The Google indexing report answers a different question about that search engine. Use each result to guide the next check for the exact URL you are reviewing.

Make on-page fixes that help the reader

Open a page before rewriting its title or main heading. Read the first paragraph and see whether it matches the promise of the title. A page called “How to choose a desk lamp” should explain how to choose one. A page called “Compact desk lamp” should make the product and its main details clear. Matching those pieces helps readers decide whether they are in the right place.

If the crawl finds repeated titles, compare the pages themselves. Some may be variations of the same product. Others may have different purposes but use the same title because of a template. Update a page title when it can describe something specific and useful. Keep the wording readable and add product details only when they belong on that page.

Review internal links after you change a section. A link from a buying guide can help readers reach the appropriate product category. A link from a product page can point to a setup guide where someone needs the next step. Use link text that describes the destination. If a link gives little context, read the sentence aloud and choose words that tell the reader where they will land.

Example of a crawl after a store update

Imagine an online store replaces its old lighting category with separate pages for desk and floor lamps. Its website audit now lists several links pointing to the old category. One appears in the main menu. Two appear in buying guides. Another appears in an email archive that the team still links to from a help page.

The editor opens each source and asks what a reader expected. The main menu can point to an updated lighting overview if there is one. A guide about a narrow desk can point to desk lamps. A guide about reading chairs can point to floor lamps. The email archive may need a short note that explains how the category changed.

The team updates the menu and guides, then opens a sample from the desktop and mobile layouts. It checks that the correct categories load and that each guide still reads naturally with the new link. It reruns a focused crawl and compares the affected URLs with its original list. If an issue remains, the team looks at the source rather than assuming the whole fix failed.

Turn audit findings into a work list

Give each task one owner and one way to confirm the fix. For a broken link, the check may be opening the source page and following the corrected link. For duplicate titles, it may be comparing a group of pages and confirming that the final titles describe their different purposes. A small, observable result makes the task easier to close.

Record dependencies. A developer may need to change a template before an editor can improve the wording across the affected pages. An editor may need a product manager to confirm the new URL before updating links. Putting those steps in order prevents two people from making separate fixes to the same issue.

Keep a note about issues you chose to leave for later. A low-priority warning may deserve review after a product launch or after a migration finishes. State why it was deferred and give it a date or condition for review. That keeps the same item from being assigned again each time the team opens the report.

Verify the work after a second crawl

Run the same crawl settings where possible. Look at the specific URLs and issue types you intended to change. A site can gain new pages between audits, so the total issue count may move for reasons that have little to do with the work you just finished. Compare the affected links directly.

Read the report beside a browser check. If the crawler still sees an old link, open the source and find where it appears. It may be in a mobile menu, a related-products card, or an old copy of the same article. Fix the shared source where appropriate, then check a few pages that use it.

Use one place to record what changed and when. Include the first report date, the change date, and the follow-up result. Where a page matters to search traffic, use Search Console when you have access to review its queries and impressions over a suitable period. Traffic can change with seasons, stock, and other site edits, so keep those dates in view when interpreting the results.

Questions about Seobility and technical SEO audits

Is a website crawler useful for a small store?

Yes, a crawler can find repeated links and issues that are easy to miss when opening pages one by one. Start with a crawl that matches the size of your store and check the pages customers depend on. Review a few examples by hand before making broad changes.

Should I fix redirects or broken links first?

Start with links that prevent people from reaching an important destination. Review redirect chains when they add steps or lead to a page that no longer serves the reader. If an old URL is still used outside your site, keep its intended redirect while updating internal links to the current page.

What should I include in a client report?

Show the affected URL, the source of the issue, the work completed, and the evidence from the follow-up check. A short note explaining why the fix mattered is often enough. Include unresolved items with an owner and a clear next step.

Can a site audit track my keyword positions?

A website audit helps you inspect pages and links. A rank tracking workflow follows a set of queries over time and can help you check which page appears. If you want to plan both tasks, see the SE Ranking guide.

What should I ask before choosing Seobility access?

Confirm the project count, crawl limits, report access, and any export feature you need. If you want to compare results over time, ask whether you can keep and revisit old crawl reports. Use a small site you have permission to audit for your first project.

A practical example for a WooCommerce store

Suppose a shop has just split its design tools category into separate pages for photo editors and stock libraries. Before running an audit, list the new category URLs, a few products in each category, and the old URL. Include a blog post that used to link to the combined category. This gives you a small set of pages with clear expectations.

Open the old category first. If it sends visitors to one of the new categories, check whether that destination matches what visitors originally wanted. If the old page served two very different needs, check the links that point to it and update each one to the best matching destination. A tutorial about editing images may need the photo editor category. A guide about finding licensed stock images may need the stock library category. The redirect helps people with old bookmarks, while direct links in current content make the new structure clearer.

Next, compare how the crawler reaches the new product pages. If most products are reached from the category and one is reachable only through the sitemap, inspect the category in a browser. Pagination, a filter, or an empty product assignment might explain the difference. Fix the root cause in WooCommerce and open the category on a phone to confirm a customer can reach the product without entering its URL by hand.

Check the preferred URL for products that can be found from more than one category. A product appearing in two categories can be useful to customers. What matters is that both category links lead to the intended product page. If the audit shows several different product URLs, look at the links and the canonical tags before changing anything. Record which URL the business wants customers and search engines to use.

Build an audit report someone can act on

A useful report tells the next person exactly where to look and how to tell whether a fix worked. For a broken internal link, record the source page, the words that form the link, the current destination, and the intended replacement. For a repeated title, add an example and note whether the title comes from a shared template or an individual page. For a URL that should be indexed, document the response code, the canonical, and any index directive you found. Those details help the developer or editor reproduce the issue.

Give each item a priority that reflects its effect on visitors. A broken link from a buying guide to a popular product needs a different response from a missing description on an old tag page. If a single menu link is broken across many pages, assign one task to fix the menu and include a few pages for the person testing the change. Counting every occurrence is useful for measuring scope. Turning every occurrence into a separate ticket makes the work harder to follow.

Schedule the next check around a real change

Run a targeted crawl after a menu change, a product migration, or a release that touches page templates. Save the earlier results so you can check the same pages with the same settings. If the new report shows fewer URLs, check whether the missing ones were intentionally retired or accidentally lost from the navigation. When you share the result, include what changed, which pages you tested, and any pages that still need a decision. That gives the team a useful record when a similar issue appears again.

Start with a crawl of the pages visitors rely on, then check broken internal links and compare the results after you update them. See Screaming Frog SEO Spider for another crawl workflow.
